div.p: The main objective of this paper is to describe several fundamental issues in the development of a practical and unified technology for building fault-tolerant, adaptive and distributed real-time intelligent decision systems (RTIDS) for monitoring and control of safety-critical real-time environments. These embedded systems include new generation airplane avionics, high-performance network and telephone switching systems, Space Station control software, weapons control systems, and medical monitoring equipments. This technology shall be based on a rigorous framework which facilitates formal verification and validation of these intelligent time-critical embedded systems. Real-time intelligent decision systems exhibit three characteristics which distinguish them from other decision systems:
(1) bounded response time, (2) adaptive to the changing environment, and
(3) fault-tolerant.

Owing to the complexity of today and future real-time environments which often necessitate smart monitoring and control systems, rule-based expert or production systems are proposed as the ideal candidate to implement these real-time intelligent decision systems. However, current expert system technology does not provide the theoretical framework nor the tools for building expert systems which satisfy the above three requirements. Hence, most current real-time decision systems are implemented in well-established conventional programming plafforms which may not exhibit the level of expertise and flexibility needed to handle unforeseen and changing system scenarios.

We have made an initial effort to tackle the difficult analysis problem of determining whether a rule-based decision system has bounded response time, but more work remain to be performed to yield a practical response time verification technology. In this paper, we describe research results and ongoing investigations concerning the analysis problem. To complement our work in response time analysis, we are currently initiating a concerted effort to develop a scientific foundation for making these intelligent decision systems adaptive as well as fault-tolerant, with the ultimate goal of building intelligent decision systems which satisfy the above three requirements.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-time intelligent decision systems (RTIDSs) are smart embedded systems which must respond to the continually changing environment being monitored and controlled within stringent timing constraints. These embedded systems include new generation airplane avionics, high-(1) bounded response time, (2) adaptive to the changing environment, and

(3) fault-tolerant. First, the real-time decision system must satisfy stringent timing constraints to respond to events in the rapidly changing environment so that the results of the decision system's computation in each monitor-decide cycle are valid in safely operating the real-time environment. A monitor-decide cycle starts with the update of the input sensor variables and ends when the decision system reaches a fixed point (a consistent evaluation of the environmental situation). The length of the monitor-decide cycle must not exceed the environmentally imposed timing constraints. The result of missing a deadline may inflict serious damage to the real-time system, and may be harmful to human operators and users. The formal verification of these real-time decision systems to ensure that they satisfy the specified integrity and timing requirements is thus essential if such systems are to be used to monitor and control safety-critical environments.

Second, the real-time decision system must continually and dynamically revise its behavior based on past state information, current sensor input, and predicted model of the environment so that its control decisions are more appropriate (in terms of logical correctness and performance) for the current behavior of the rapidly changing external environment being monitored and controlled. This requires continuous modification and/or reconfiguration of the knowledge base of the decision system while maintaining the system's consistency and timeliness.

Third, the real-time decision system must be able to tolerate and recover from different kinds of faults (either unforeseen or anticipated) caused by the external environment or by the embedded real-time system itself. Techniques such as self-stabilization, roll-back error recovery, distributed agreement, transient error detection, algorithmbased fault-tolerance and software/hardware redundancy may need to be integrated and applied systematically to attain the desired degree of fault-tolerance and reliability.

Owing to the complexity of today and future real-time environments which often necessitate smart monitoring and control systems, rule-based expert or production systems are proposed as the ideal candidate to implement these real-time intelligent decision systems. However, current expert systems technology does not provide the theoretical framework nor the tools necessary for building large-scale expert systems which satisfy the above three requirements. Hence, most current real-time decision sys-tems are implemented in conventional programming platforms which may not exhibit the level of expertise and flexibility needed to handle unforeseen and changing realtime system scenarios. Research in real-time rule-based expert sy,stems has gained considerable importance in the last few ye&, e.g., [Benda 871, [Hayes-Roth 901, [Koch et al 861, [Laffey et al. 881, [Marsh 881, [Muratore et al 901, [O'Reilly & Cromarty 853, and [Payton & Bihari 911. However, there has been little work in the formal verification and validation of expert systems in the real-time environment. Most studies deal with narrow application domains or with optimization of expert systems and planninglsearching without regard to hard response time guarantees. The lack of concrete results in response time guarantees for real-time expert systems is partly due to the fact that determining how fast an expert system can respond under all possible situations is a difficult and in general an undecidable problem. To tackle this problem, we have developed a powerful and efficient analysis methodology for a large class of rule-based equational logic (EQL) programs in order to determine whether a program in this class has bounded response time [Browne, Cheng & Mok 881. In particular, we have identified several sets of general behavioral constraint assertions called special forms of rules with the following property: an EQL program which satisfies all constraints in one of these sets of constraint assertions is guaranteed to have bounded response time.

We have implemented an extremely fast response time analysis algorithm which exploits the application of these special forms. Under appropriate conditions, this General Analysis Algorithm performs an entirely syntactic and/or semantic check on an EQL expert system without analyzing its corresponding state space graph in order to determine whether the expert system has bounded response time, thus avoiding the so-called combinatorial explosion problem. An invocation of an EQL rule-based program can be thought of as tracing a path in the state space graph of the program. Certain classes of OPS5 and CLIPS rulebased programs also can be analyzed with this algorithm by first translating them into equivalent EQL versions. A conventional state-space-based analysis algorithm, however, has to check in the worst case that every path from each possible initial state in the state space graph leads to a terminating state within a bounded number of steps. When an expert system is found to violate the specified timing constraints, one may wish to optimize the expert system by modifying its rule base to meet the timing constraints while satisfying the original functional specifications. We have shown the complexity of the optimization problem to be NP-hard. Therefore, we focus on efficient solutions to certain practical classes of this problem. A preliminary suite of computer-aided design (CAD) tools based on this analysis approach have been implemented and their capability has been demonstrated in [Browne,Cheng & Mok 881 and [Cheng & Wang 901 by the successful analysis of a number of industrial real-time expert systems developed by NASA and Mitre [Helly 841,[Marsh 881.

To further enhance the applicability of our analysis technique, we have introduced a facility for the rule-based programmer to specify application-specific knowledge to the analysis tool in order to validate the performance of an even wider range of programs [Cheng et al911. The idea is to provide the rule-based ro ammer the Estella language which has been designed for %e specification of behavioral constraint assertions about rule-based EQL programs. These application-specific assertions capture the require-ments for achieving certain performance levels for a rulebased program in a particular application tbat are too difficult to be detected mechanically and assist the analysis tool in checking whether an EQL program has bounded response time. The Estella-General Analysis Tool highlights our effort to develop practical tools that work on large-scale, real systems rather than to invent a theoretical analysis approach which does not scale up to analyze large realistic systems.

With the introduction of this new analysis technique and the accompanying specification facility, we have just embarked to develop a formal and practical framework for the rigorous analysis and formal verification of rule-based expert systems used to monitor and control real-time applications. A great deal of research work remain to be done before we can rely on expert systems to perform intelligent tasks in bounded time. To build expert systems for monitoring and controlling a real-time environment where faults can occur and whose behavior can change constantly, we need to go beyond formal analysis and verification. We need to develop a solid scientific foundation for building adaptive and fault-tolerant real-time expert decision systems with bounded response time.

The remainder of this section briefly describes the EQL rule-based language and outlines the new analysis technique, Section 2 outlines basic issues in bounded response time analysis and synthesis. Section 3 describes the design issues for RTIDSs and outlines promising approaches for solving problems in the design of high-performance, adaptive and fault-tolerant RTIDSs. Section 4 is the conclusion.

div.head: The Basic Real-Time EQL Rule-Based Language
div.p: An EQL program consists of a finite set of rules (consisting of m single-assignment subrules) each of which is of the form: al := bl ! . . e ! a,,, := b , IF EC A rule has three parts: (1) LHS: the left-hand-side of the multiple assignment statement, i.e., the ais, (2) RHS: the right-hand-side of the multiple assignment statement, i.e., the bis, and (3) EC: the enabling condition. An enabling condition is a predicate on the variables in the program. A rule is enabled if its enabling condition becomes true. A rule firing is the execution of the multiple assignment statement. A rule is jirable only when it is enabled and by firing it will change the value of some variable in LHS. A multiple assignment statement assigns values to one or more variables in parallel. The RHS expressions must be side-effect free. The execution of a multiple assignment statement consists of the evaluation of all the RHS expressions, followed by updating the LHS variables with the values of the corresponding expressions. An invocation of an EQL program is a sequence of rule firings. When two or more rules are enabled, the selection of which rule to h e is nondeterministic or up to the run-time scheduler, but any rule that stays firable must eventually be fired. An EQL program is said to have reached a fixed point when none of its rules are firable. An EQL program is said to always reach a fixed point in bounded time iff the number of rule firings needed to take the program from an initial state to a fixed point is always bounded by a fixed upper bound. This bound is imposed by performance constraints. First, unlike programs written in a procedural language, the control flow of expert system programs is embedded in the data and cannot be easily derived. It can also be implementation dependent. Second, the contents of the working memory of an expert system change continually with each rule firing. In the real-time control environment, there is the added complexity of timing constraints which makes the development of correct real-time programs more difficult even if such programs are written in procedural languages.

div.head: More Expressive MRL Production Systems
div.p: The syntax of MRL programs Wang, Mok & Cheng 901 is an extension of that of EQL programs. What distinguishes MRL from EQL is the use of macro variables, which are similar to the working memory in OPS5. Each macro variable represents a set of primitive variables called expanded variables or working memory elements (wme). Rules that contain macro variables are mucro rules, in contrast to plain rules in EQL programs. Conceptually, we model the execution of MRL, programs as follows. Before execution, a macro rule is expanded to a set of plain rules each of which contains one of the possible combinations of macro variable expansions, i.e., each macro variable is instantiated to one of the corresponding expanded variables. The result of the expansion is an equivalent EQL program which has the same behavior as the MRL program. Macro variables m,ake it more convenient to assemble related input data into data structures, and also allow us to introduce logical quantifiers, either existential quantifiers or universal quant@ers, into MRL. The combination of macro variables and logical quantifiers makes MRL a sufficiently powerful production language for writing OPSS-type porgy 811 real-time expert systems. div.head: Issues in the Design of Adaptive and Fault-Tolerant RTIDSs
div.p: This section describes the key problems and outlines promising approaches for solving these problems in the design of high-performance, adaptive and fault-tolerant real-time decision systems.

div.head: Parallel Execution of Rule-Rased Expert Systems
div.p: Parallel execution is explored as an approach to achieve higher execution speed in production systems used in domains requiring high perfonnance and real-time response. Unfortunately, OPSS-based expert systems do not lend themselves to even a moderate degree of parallelism (usually at most ten-folds) [Gupta 871. In [Cheng 91b1, we describe how rule-firing parallelism can be automatically extracted from production systems. The proposed technique is successfully applied to reduce the execution time of two NASA production systems. This ruleparallelism extraction technique complements the parallel matching technique in [Gupta 871. It also complements the parallel firing techniques in [Ishida 9 11 by breaking a large production system into smaller, more manageable rule clusters, each of which can be further analyzed for potential parallel rule firings.

Our ongoing work considers the implementation of an efficient computational environment for parallel execution of production systems, and investigates further improvement of our proposed technique for the automated extraction of parallelism. Since our proposed technique is designed for the experimental EQL language, we would like to study the applicability of this technique to other expert system shells. Furthermore, we are developing techniques for solving the following problems: (1) How to reduce the number and the size of the interfering rule sets by rewriting the given production system so that parallelism can be further increased? (2) Given a fixed number of processors, determine an optimal way to allocate the parallel modules into these n processors such that the time needed to compute the respective fixed points of all parallel modules is minimized. Solutions to these and other related problems are needed to make production systems vuly capable of operating in high performance and realtime environments.

div.head: Fault Tolerance
div.p: The faults occurring in the real-time environment which affect the decision system and those occurring within the real-time decision system can be modeled by the state space graph of the decision system. A tuple is a normal state if it appears on a path from an initial state to a fixed point. A normal state is safe (unsafe) if the behavior of the environment is (is not) consistent with the specified safety and progress requirements. Tuples which are not normal states are abnormal states.

Extemal faults are those that occur in the environment and their behavior are not consistent with the goal of the decision system, e.g., certain safety properties have been violated. Internal faults are those that occur within the real-time decision system and they may be caused by faulty decision system's design or by the environment being monitored and controlled, e.g., some variables have been corrupted as a result of hardware fault. In the absence of intemal faults, the variables of a decision system are by definition always in normal states. Furthermore, in the absence of extenial faults, the variables of a decision system are always in safe normal states. When the variables of a decision system is in an abnormal state, firing of the enabled rules may or may not bring the decision system back to a normal state.

To model the effect of faults in the state space graph, we define a deviation function 2 which maps each normal state into a set D, of tuples which may be normal or abnormal states. This function allows us to model a single fault or arbitrarily many types of faults depending on the reliability of the softwarehardware as well as the degree of faulttolerance desired. For instance, in the case where faults can have arbitrary effects on the variables, D, may be the entire set of tuples in a program's state space, Intuitively, if a fault occurs when the decision system is in state s, then the system will be in one of the states specified by Z(s).

In the case of decision systems whose faults can be modeled by the above technique, our objective is to develop recovery mechanisms which guarantee that these decision systems can recover automatically from transient intemal faults. For our purpose, we define a recovery function R which maps an abnormal state into a subset D, of the normal states. Our goal is to extend a non-fault-tolerant decision system so that if a transient internal fault occurs and uts the decision system in an abnormal state s, then fur-&er execution of the decision system will bring the system back to a state in R ( s ) within a bounded number of rule firings.

The technique of self-stabilization [Dijksua 741 has recently been re-examined to make distributed system programs more robust. We believe self-stabilization also can be applied systematically to make real-time decision systems fault-tolerant to transient intemal faults. In particular, a decision system can be made self-stabilizing if for all abnormal states, D, is the entire set of normal states. A program p is called self-stabilizing if and only if for each pair of distinct fixed points s1 and s2 of p , there is at least one input variable whose value in sI is different from its value in s2. In other words, the fixed point that a selfstabilizing program p can reach starting from any state s, depends solely on the values of the input variables in s and not on the values of the non-input variables in s. Therefore, if program p is at a fixed point and the values of one or more non-input variables change due to some faults, p is guaranteed to converge back to the same fixed point so long as the values of its input variables remain unchanged.

In [Cheng 92b1, we describe a technique for transforming any non-self-stabilizing EQL program in a special form into one that is self-stabilizing. Furthermore, we show that any self-stabilizing program obtained from a non-selfstabilizing program with bounded response time using this method also has bounded response time.

div.head: Adaptivity
div.p: Consider an adaptive real-time intelligent decision system D used to monitor and control an environment E. At time to, D starts its operation exhibiting system behavior DBo.

The behavior of a system at certain time t depends on the system's rule base at time t. Suppose the behavior of E changes from EBo to EB1 in the time interval [to, tll. Note that the change may occur slowly from to to tl or it may occur abruptly at around t l . In either case, the decision system detects b e new environmental behavior at time t l . Before t l , the changes in the environment have not been considered yet to be a change in behavior but rather changes in certain environmental factors by the decision system and thus no adaptive action requiring rule base revision needs to be taken prior to t 1.

Having detected the change in environmental behavior at t l , D begins to adapt to the new environmental behavior EBI by revising D's rule base to exhibit a more appropriate new behavior LIB1. This rule base revision occurs in the time interval [tl t z ] . Two major research problems need to be solved in order to guarantee bounded-time adaptivity.

First, we need to develop automated transformation techniques for dynamically revising the rule base. This may involve simply the activation of some previously inactive rule base modules and the deactivation of some currently active rule base modules, or it may require actual modification of certain parts of the active rule base. Second, we need to ensure that the time interval [tl, t2] required for system's adaptation is within the time constraint imposed by the environment. Exceeding the time constraint may seriously degrade system's performance and may threatens environmental safety. Both of these problems are nontrivial even in narrow application domains. We shall develop a general system and language model for studying these problems, and then implement techniques based on this model for decisiion systems in specific applications. The following example illustrates an adaptive real-time intelligent decision system.

div.head: Example 3.
div.p: Suppose we have a robotic vehicle which can navigate autonomously in unpopulated rural area as well as in urban roads. The goal of the vehicle is to move from point A located in a rural area to point B located in an urban area. The vehicle has never traversed the route from A to B and it does not have a map instructing how the travel should be made. Furthermore, the vehicle does not know how long it takes to reach the urban area and how long it takes to reach point B. The only real-time information available to the vehicle is the current distance from itself to point B as measured by the vehicle's radar system. Traffic signals are absent and roads are two-way in the rural area whereas traffic signals are everywhere and roads may be one-way in the urban area. One obvious safety requirement is that the vehicle never collides with a fixed obstacle (such as the curbside or a mountain) or with a moving obstacle (such as a pedestrian or another vehicle).

When the vehicle starts its journey from point A at time to, its decision system exhibits behavior LIBo. The rule base at time to contains rules to ensure the vehicle does not hit an obstacle but does not contain rules to check whether the road is a one-way road or whether the traffic light is green. Thus the rule base at to is appropriate for the rural area since rules for checking irrelevant issues (traffic lights and road directions) are absent or deactivated and thus the overall decision system's performance is optimized. As soon as the vehicle enters the borderline (which may not be clearcut) between the rural area and the suburban area indicated by the appearance of a traffic signal or of more moving obstacles (other vehicles and pedestrian) at time tl, the decision system revises its rule base by creating new rules and/or activating previously inactive rule base modules as well as by deactivating some original rules if necessary. The rule base is adapted to the new environment at time t2 by exhibiting a new behavior DB1 which considers traffic signals and road directions before making a navigational decision. Obviously, the decision system must adapt to the new environment fast enough to ensure the safety of the vehicle and the environment.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The main focus of this paper is to address the design issues of real-time intelligent decision systems. We have provided a formal framework for investigating this question for equational rule-based programs. Our formulation makes use of the state space representation of rule-based programs and relates the response time of a system to the length of paths to Exed points in the state space graph. To support the development of real-time intelligent decision systems with stringent timing and integrity constraints, issues of parallel execution, efficient architecture, and fault tolerance need to be resolved before we can rely on computers to perform intelligent tasks in bounded time.
